items.stem: Define the term "historical context".
items.answer: The events, conditions and ideas of the period in which a text was produced
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the events, conditions and ideas of the period in which a text was produced. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the meaning of a text can change over time.
items.answer: Readers in later periods bring different values and knowledge, and events after publication may change the significance of a text's language and images.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Readers in later periods bring different values and knowledge, and events after publication may change the significance of a text's language and images. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Diego writes: "Texts from the past should be judged only by the values of their own time." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Readers can recognise a text's original context while still critically evaluating its values from a present perspective; both readings are valid if supported.
items.markingKey: Readers can recognise a text's original context while still critically evaluating its values from a present perspective; both readings are valid if supported. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following photograph and caption from a contemporary documentary series on fast fashion, described in words.

[A young woman sits at a sewing machine in a long row of identical machines under flickering fluorescent light. In the blurred foreground lies a heap of bright T-shirts with price tags reading '4.99'.]
Caption: 'Shift 2 of 2. Rina, 19, sews 120 collars an hour.'

How might a reader at the time of production and a reader today respond differently to this text?
items.answer: A shopper may feel guilt; an economist may argue the jobs still matter to the local economy.
items.markingKey: A shopper may feel guilt; an economist may argue the jobs still matter to the local economy. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column published in a national newspaper.

Let me be clear: I am no technophobe. I file this column from a laptop, on a train, while my phone buzzes like a trapped wasp. But I have watched my own students in Nairobi sit side by side at lunch, heads bowed, in total silence, as if at a funeral. We would never let a casino open in a school corridor. Why, then, do we allow a slot machine in every pocket?

Explain how the context of the text shapes its meaning or its reception.
items.answer: Written during a public debate about phone bans in schools; the columnist's identity as a teacher in Nairobi gives first-hand authority.
items.markingKey: Written during a public debate about phone bans in schools; the columnist's identity as a teacher in Nairobi gives first-hand authority. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Choose a non-literary body of work you have studied (for example a set of posters or photographs from one period). Analyse how context shapes the representation of a group within it.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A text cannot be understood without knowing its historical context."
items.answer: Context deepens understanding but is not always essential; the strongest readings combine close reading with contextual insight.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains allusions and purpose; misreadings occur without it. Arguments against: many texts remain powerful across time; close reading reveals much. Supported judgement: Context deepens understanding but is not always essential; the strongest readings combine close reading with contextual insight. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Briefly explain why context should be integrated into analysis rather than added as background.
items.answer: Context is only valuable when it explains a specific choice or effect; a separate history lesson does not show how the text creates meaning.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A one-sided presentation that favours a particular viewpoint"?
items.answer: bias

items.stem: A student claims: "A news report that contains no opinions is unbiased." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Bias can operate through selection, order, sources and connotation, even when no explicit opinion is stated.
items.markingKey: Bias can operate through selection, order, sources and connotation, even when no explicit opinion is stated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why headlines are powerful in shaping opinion.
items.answer: Many readers only see the headline, so its wording and framing determine the impression of the event.

items.stem:
Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Analyse the effect of the choice of grammatical subject in the text.
items.answer: The choice of grammatical subject: A makes students the active subject with a goal; B makes the "mob" the cause of chaos and shoppers the victims.
items.markingKey: The choice of grammatical subject: A makes students the active subject with a goal; B makes the "mob" the cause of chaos and shoppers the victims. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following news report from an international news website.

Headline: Floods sweep through Kerala villages as monsoon intensifies
Standfirst: Thousands evacuated; state officials warn more rain is expected
Rescue teams in fishing boats ferried residents from rooftops on Tuesday after three days of heavy rain. "We lost everything except our lives," said Leela Menon, 63, holding a plastic bag of documents. The meteorological department has issued a red alert for six districts.

Guiding question: How does the report balance information and human interest?
Write one analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question, using at least two references to the text.
items.answer: Thesis: the report uses news conventions to inform and a single human voice to move. (1) Headline verb and standfirst. (2) Inverted pyramid. (3) The quotation and concrete detail. Evaluation: one quoted victim may stand in for many, and the framing focuses on disaster rather than causes.

(3) The quotation and concrete detail. Evaluation: one quoted victim may stand in for many, and the framing focuses on disaster rather than causes. Markbands (criteria A–D). items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "editorial".

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

The words "we are the present, standing in water" are an example of which feature?
items.answer: metaphor
items.markingKey: A. "we are the present, standing in water" is an example of metaphor: it overturns the cliché "you are the future" and makes the crisis immediate and physical.

items.stem: Briefly explain why political speeches use repetition.
items.answer: Speeches are heard once; repetition helps listeners remember key ideas, builds rhythm and emotion and creates a sense of unity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Speeches are heard once; repetition helps listeners remember key ideas, builds rhythm and emotion and creates a sense of unity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Explain how the context of the text shapes its meaning or its reception.
items.answer: In the Second World War many governments ran poster campaigns to bring women into factories while men served in the armed forces.
items.markingKey: In the Second World War many governments ran poster campaigns to bring women into factories while men served in the armed forces. items.stem: A student claims: "Emotional appeals in speeches are always manipulative." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Pathos can be legitimate when it reflects real stakes; it becomes manipulative when it replaces evidence or exploits fear.

items.stem: Explain why the caption of a documentary photograph matters.
items.answer: The caption anchors meaning, identifies (or fails to identify) subjects and frames how the viewer interprets the image.

items.stem:
Read the following description of Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' (1936) with its original caption.

[A black-and-white photograph. A woman in worn clothes sits under a tent, her hand raised to her chin, her eyes looking past the camera with a worried expression. Two children lean on her shoulders, faces turned away; a baby lies in her lap. The frame is tight, cutting out the surroundings.]
Caption (US Farm Security Administration file): 'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children. Age thirty-two. Nipomo, California.'

Explain the effect of the caption as anchorage in this photograph.
items.answer: Caption as anchorage: "'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children.'" – the terse caption fixes the meaning as poverty and dignity, but reduces the woman to a type.

items.stem: Explain the difference between propaganda and persuasion.
items.answer: Persuasion openly tries to convince through argument and appeal; propaganda systematically manipulates, often by distorting or omitting information, usually for a political or state agenda.

items.stem: Distinguish between advertising photography and documentary photography.
items.answer: Documentary photography claims to record reality, often for social purposes; advertising photography is staged to sell, constructing idealised scenes.

items.stem: Distinguish between historical context and cultural context.
items.answer: Historical context concerns events and conditions of a time (a war, an election); cultural context concerns beliefs, customs and values of a community (attitudes to gender, religion).

items.stem: Explain the difference between bias and framing.
items.answer: Bias is a one-sided slant in favour of a view; framing is the broader process of selecting and emphasising aspects of an issue. Framing can produce bias but is present in all reporting.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in an English-language newspaper in Lisbon.

My grandmother's street in Alfama now has eleven bakeries and no neighbours. The bakeries sell pastéis de nata to people who will leave on Sunday; the neighbours who once bought bread there have left for good, priced out by short-term rentals. Tourism, we are told, is our salvation. Perhaps. But a city that sells its every doorway eventually has nothing left to show its visitors except itself, emptied.

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To argue that unregulated tourism and short-term rentals are hollowing out historic neighbourhoods. Supporting feature: "Tourism, we are told, is our salvation" (irony) – "we are told" distances the writer from the official claim and signals disbelief.
items.markingKey: To argue that unregulated tourism and short-term rentals are hollowing out historic neighbourhoods. items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

How might knowledge of the context of production help a reader to interpret this speech?
items.answer: In Edwardian Britain women could not vote in parliamentary elections; some property-owning women over 30 gained the vote in 1918 and equal franchise came in 1928. Suffragettes were often described as unreasonable or hysterical in the press.
items.markingKey: In Edwardian Britain women could not vote in parliamentary elections; some property-owning women over 30 gained the vote in 1918 and equal franchise came in 1928. Suffragettes were often described as unreasonable or hysterical in the press. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

With reference to the guiding question – "How does the mayor construct the library as a place of belonging?" – write the thesis and first body paragraph of a Paper 1 guided analysis.
items.answer: Thesis: the mayor presents the library as a human, multilingual home rather than a store of information. (1) Code-switching in the greeting includes migrant communities. (2) Anaphora and personification contrast the phone's limits with human care (the child, the nurse). (3) The final possessive "belongs to you" transfers ownership to residents. Evaluation: the speech is inclusive but sentimental; it avoids questions of funding.

items.stem: "Emotional appeals in speeches are always manipulative." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Pathos can be legitimate when it reflects real stakes; it becomes manipulative when it replaces evidence or exploits fear.
items.markingKey: Pathos can be legitimate when it reflects real stakes; it becomes manipulative when it replaces evidence or exploits fear. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between documentary photography and advertising photography.
items.answer: Documentary photography claims to record reality, often for social purposes; advertising photography is staged to sell, constructing idealised scenes.
items.markingKey: Documentary photography claims to record reality, often for social purposes; advertising photography is staged to sell, constructing idealised scenes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between cultural context and historical context.
items.answer: Historical context concerns events and conditions of a time (a war, an election); cultural context concerns beliefs, customs and values of a community (attitudes to gender, religion).
items.markingKey: Historical context concerns events and conditions of a time (a war, an election); cultural context concerns beliefs, customs and values of a community (attitudes to gender, religion). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why quoting an eyewitness is effective in a news report.
items.answer: It adds human interest and emotional impact and gives the appearance of authenticity while the reporter remains neutral.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It adds human interest and emotional impact and gives the appearance of authenticity while the reporter remains neutral. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

Analyse how the phrase "You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps" contributes to the writer's purpose.
items.answer: Antithesis: "You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps" – the contrast sets abstract political time against concrete domestic loss and divides "you" (leaders) from "we" (the young).
items.markingKey: Antithesis: "You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps" – the contrast sets abstract political time against concrete domestic loss and divides "you" (leaders) from "we" (the young). Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A photograph shows exactly what happened." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Framing, cropping, timing and selection shape what is shown; photographs are constructed representations.
items.markingKey: Framing, cropping, timing and selection shape what is shown; photographs are constructed representations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

How might a reader at the time of production and a reader today respond differently to this text?
items.answer: Sympathetic listeners hear moral clarity; others may hear disrespect for diplomacy – the speech deliberately risks this to be heard.
items.markingKey: Sympathetic listeners hear moral clarity; others may hear disrespect for diplomacy – the speech deliberately risks this to be heard. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Outline the purpose of the text and the means by which it pursues that purpose.
items.answer: Both inform readers of the protest, but each frames it to shape the reader's attitude – sympathetic (A) or hostile (B). Supporting feature: "to demand rent controls" (purpose clause) – Newspaper A states the protesters' aim, presenting them as rational citizens.
items.markingKey: Both inform readers of the protest, but each frames it to shape the reader's attitude – sympathetic (A) or hostile (B). Supporting feature: "to demand rent controls" (purpose clause) – Newspaper A states the protesters' aim, presenting them as rational citizens. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Explain one way in which the context in which this text appears affects its message.
items.answer: In the Second World War many governments ran poster campaigns to bring women into factories while men served in the armed forces.
items.markingKey: In the Second World War many governments ran poster campaigns to bring women into factories while men served in the armed forces. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following description of Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' (1936) with its original caption.

[A black-and-white photograph. A woman in worn clothes sits under a tent, her hand raised to her chin, her eyes looking past the camera with a worried expression. Two children lean on her shoulders, faces turned away; a baby lies in her lap. The frame is tight, cutting out the surroundings.]
Caption (US Farm Security Administration file): 'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children. Age thirty-two. Nipomo, California.'

Analyse how the visual elements of the text contribute to its meaning.
items.answer: The hand at the chin, the triangular composition and the turned-away children concentrate emotion on the mother's face; black-and-white tones emphasise documentary seriousness.
items.markingKey: The hand at the chin, the triangular composition and the turned-away children concentrate emotion on the mother's face; black-and-white tones emphasise documentary seriousness. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Evaluate how far a reader needs to know the context to understand this text.
items.answer: News outlets often reflect the values of their owners and readerships; protest coverage shows how framing shapes public opinion.

Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Journalism can never be truly objective."
items.answer: Complete objectivity is impossible, but fairness and accuracy are achievable standards that matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every report involves selection and framing; journalists have contexts. Arguments against: professional standards and verification reduce bias; fact and opinion can still be distinguished. Supported judgement: Complete objectivity is impossible, but fairness and accuracy are achievable standards that matter. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: "The rhetoric of political speeches has changed little over time." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Core devices persist, but medium and audience have reshaped length, register and delivery.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: classical devices (tricolon, anaphora) persist; appeals to ethos, pathos, logos are timeless. Arguments against: media changed delivery (radio, TV, social media); shorter soundbites dominate now.
